pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 90: Growing: nothing. Wilting: everything. (My fault.)*

Nadia Okafor tapped her pen on my desk. She had a bright blue hair clip and a smile that looked like it had been tested for accuracy. "Friday," she said. "Sleepover. Your parents are okay?"

I looked at my hand. I was holding a ruler, measuring the width of my math book, which was a useless thing to do but my hands needed to be busy. "Yes," I said. "Mama is on night shift, but she leaves at six. Baba is at the bakery until noon."

"Great. I'll bring the board games." She moved on to the next kid.

I stood up, my knees feeling wobbly, like they had forgotten how to support a body. "Yes," I said again. "I mean, that sounds good. Friday is fine."

I walked to the window. The car park was grey and empty. My heart was doing a strange, fluttering thing in my chest, like a moth trapped in a tin. I had a friend. A real one. In this city.

Then I remembered the clock.

Friday dusk is a watering. Saturday dawn is a watering.

I looked at the ruler in my hand, then at the grey sky. I did the math. I had two waterings to miss. Two times the garden would go thirsty. Two times I would be the one to blame.

I put the ruler back in my pocket. My hand was shaking.
pages.image: Sana, thin with brown skin and round glasses, stands in a classroom doorway holding a ruler, looking worried; a girl with a blue hair clip smiles at her from a desk nearby.

pages.text:
I told Theo I would handle it. He was leaning against the hedge, pushing his sleeves up over his elbows. He looked at me, then at the wilting basil in the corner. "You sure?" he asked. His voice was flat.

"I am," I said. "I have a schedule. I wrote it down." I showed him the note on my denim jacket pocket. It was just two lines: *5 PM. 5 AM.*

He nodded slowly. "Okay."

The party was loud. It was not like the movies. It was messy and sticky and smelled of pizza and sweat. We played charades. I did not know the words. I flapped my hands and made faces, and I was terrible at it. But then, for one minute, Nadia laughed at my bad guess, and Theo snorted, and the sun came through the window and hit my shoulder, warm and golden.

I stopped breathing. The noise of the room faded. I was not thinking about the clock or the roots. I was just there, in the circle of people, feeling the heat on my skin. It was perfect. It was the best minute of my life.

Then someone yelled "Sana, it's your turn!" and the minute was gone.
pages.image: Sana sits on a carpet in a messy living room, laughing with a group of friends during a game; sunlight streams through a window onto her shoulder, highlighting her round glasses and denim jacket.

pages.text:
Saturday morning was cold. The wind cut through my jacket, which still smelled like pizza and other people's shampoo. I walked home, my boots crunching on the wet leaves, tired in a way that sleep would not fix.

I reached the gap in the fence and crawled through. The air in the Summer Room was wrong. It did not smell like lemons and heat. It smelled like dust and dryness.

The tomato plants were brown, their leaves hanging limp and dead to touch the soil. A lemon lay on the ground, dry and wrinkled. The whole room looked thin, as if the color had been drained out of it.

Theo was there. He was on his knees, holding a watering can. He looked exhausted, his hands black with dirt. He did not look up.

"I tried," he said, his voice rough. "I came early. I watered them. But it was too late for half of them."

I looked at the dead plants, then down at my shoes. I had forgotten.
pages.image: Sana and Theo, a boy in a beanie and hoodie, kneel in a dusty garden filled with brown, wilting tomato plants; Theo holds a watering can, looking down at the dry soil.

pages.text:
"I am sorry," I said. The words came out small and flat, which was not how I had planned to sound at all.

Theo shrugged, a quick, sharp movement that looked like he was snapping a dry twig. "It is fine," he said, though the tightness in his jaw said otherwise. He looked at the broken stems, then at me, and he did not look angry. He just looked tired, the way I look when I have run out of juice boxes.

Gherkin was on the bench. He moved his head very slowly toward us, blinking with a deliberate, heavy slowness, like the shutter of a cheap camera closing on a bad photo.

"Mm," he said, his voice low and dry. "This is what happens."

I waited for him to be mad, or for a punishment to arrive, but he did not even look at the brown plants. He looked at me.

"The garden did not punish you," Gherkin said. "The water did not come. The plants did not drink. It is only arithmetic."

He turned his head back to the sun. "Mm. Not yet."
pages.image: Gherkin, an old mossy tortoise, sits on a wooden bench in a garden, looking calmly at two children; the background shows wilted brown plants and grey light.

pages.text:
I sat down in the dust. My knees hit the dry earth. I picked up a brown leaf. It crumbled under my fingers.

I did not cry loudly. I did not make a sound. But my eyes burned, and my chest felt tight, like a zipper stuck halfway down a jacket. I looked at the dead tomato plants. They were not broken because I was bad. They were broken because I was not there.

I thought about the minute at the party. The warmth on my shoulder. The laughter. I had let that minute matter more than the roots.

Responsibility does not feel like being good. It feels like carrying a full bucket of water when your arms are shaking. It feels like the silence after you forget.

I put the leaf back on the ground. I looked at Theo. He was still kneeling. I reached out and touched his sleeve. He did not pull away.

The garden was quiet. The magic was not gone, but it was waiting. And I was the one who had to make it happen.
pages.image: Sana sits in the dusty soil of a garden, looking down at her hands; a boy in a beanie kneels nearby, and an old tortoise rests on a bench in the background.
